planting.note: Divide dormant rhizome clumps in early fall and replant into deep, well-drained sandy soil with a thin organic duff layer, since this species resents heavy clay and standing moisture.

directions: Hexastylis sorriei is a critically rare heartleaf ginger restricted to the fire-maintained longleaf pine sandhills around Fort Bragg and Camp Mackall in North Carolina. Divide rhizome clumps in fall and set them into deep, well-drained sandy soil, mimicking the dappled light beneath an open pine-and-wiregrass canopy rather than deep forest shade. Established plants form a low, slow-spreading mat of leathery, mottled heart-shaped leaves that persists through winter. Because wild populations are extremely limited, only plant nursery-propagated material and never collect from the wild.

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections after flowering and reset them just below the surface in humus-rich, evenly moist soil; this cold-hardy Japanese species tolerates harsher winters than most Asian wild gingers.

directions: Asarum megacalyx is a cold-hardy woodland wild ginger from the mountains of northern Honshu, Japan, where it grows under deciduous forest canopy that stays cool and moist through summer. Divide rhizome sections after flowering and tuck them just below the soil surface in humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil that never fully dries out. The glossy, heart-shaped leaves emerge with a faint patterning in spring before settling into solid dark green, and the oversized purple-brown flowers sit low in the foliage at ground level. It takes colder winters better than many of its Chinese relatives, making it a reasonable choice for northern shade gardens.

planting.note: Divide rooted rhizome sections in spring and replant shallowly in loose, humus-rich, evenly moist soil beneath a closed canopy; avoid letting the planting site dry out while new roots establish.

directions: Asarum caudigerum hails from shaded woodland slopes in Sichuan and Yunnan, China, where it spreads slowly through leaf litter and loose, humus-rich soil. Propagate by dividing rooted rhizome sections in spring and replanting them shallowly in evenly moist, well-drained soil under a closed canopy. The broad evergreen leaves are covered in fine hairs, especially on the undersides and stems, giving the foliage a soft texture that sets it apart from smoother-leaved wild gingers. Its tailed, mottled flowers are borne low among the foliage in spring and are easy to miss without parting the leaves to look at ground level.
